speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been widely reported in the press that a number of crop wipe-outs last spring were caused by the federal law that forbids the use of non-metric units of measurement on labels, in this case those on containers of agricultural chemicals. Further crop damage is predicted for the coming spring if these federal regulations remain in force.
We have already established that the welfare of the country, or of individual Canadians, is of absolutely no consequence to the Government if it conflicts with Government plans or policy. Nevertheless these are the things with which we here have been elected to deal, and I am certain that there are those on the Government side of the House, even, who share this sense of responsibility. I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm):
That this mindless, headlong rush into metrication be tempered with a little sober second thought, and specifically, that double labelling on all potentially hazardous material be not only permitted but encouraged.

He writes:
Dear Bill:
I will be brief. My whole operation is in jeopardy. Canada Post has delayed new orders, the banks have repossessed my sleigh, the elves are on strike because of six and five, I can't collect unemployment benefits because I'm a seasonal, part-time worker, and Mrs. Claus wants to move to Florida; but, with a deindexed pension who can afford it?
This Government has really taken the HO out of my HO! HO! HO! The Prime Minister promised a Royal Commission but there seems to be a waiting list. Mr. Ouellet won't lift a finger until I metrify the odometers on the reindeer and, to top it all off, Herb Gray threatened to make me a Crown corporation: Santa Canada.
Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That we listen to old Saint Nick's message and appoint him to the Senate.

subsubtopic: OECD UNEMPLOYMENT FORECAST-REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF BUDGET
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who knows that at two o'clock today the OECD report was officially tabled. In view of the fact that that report shows that unemployment in Canada will likely hit 13.25 per cent in the beginning of next year, meaning a jump of a further 60,000 people out of work, and a rate of unemployment of 13.25 per cent compared with a 24-nation OECD average of 9.5 per cent, would the Minister of Finance tell us whether he would be willing to bring in, at the earliest possible opportunity, a new budget, so that this tragedy which is being inflicted upon Canadian workers may be brought to an early halt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: OECD UNEMPLOYMENT FORECAST-REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is referring to a forecast. As he knows, a lot of forecasts made in the last few years have been proven

December 22, 1982
Oral Questions
wrong on the optimistic side. This one is particularly pessimistic. We hope that it will be proven wrong as previous optimistic forecasts were proven wrong.
As the Eton. Member also knows, a number of forecasts have been made by private Canadian institutions over the last few months. These forecasts all indicate that unemployment in Canada will remain high in the next year, that we can expect a gradual decline of unemployment during the course of the year, and a gradual recovery. The forecasts for recovery vary between institutions, but up to now all institutions which have made forecasts in Canada for the next year forecast a positive rate of growth.
1 have indicated that I am considering bringing in a new budget early in the new year, before the beginning of the fiscal year. I certainly intend to proceed with that plan, but I stress to the Elon. Member that no budget by itself could radically change the situation which we are experiencing at the present time, not only in Canada but in most industrialized countries. This will have to take place as part of a broad policy, not only in Canada but in other countries, involving not only budgetary policies but all other elements of the economy.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, again my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who stated that perhaps forecasts will not become reality. Let us deal with reality, because OECD deals with reality and points out that in real gross national product terms Canada had a negative, a minus 5 per cent reduction last year, even behind Turkey, for example, which had a better record; in fact Canada had the worst record of any OECD country-24 out of 24. In view of the fact that that is costing every worker in Canada $100 a month in current dollars, would the Minister of Finance indicate, first, what is the depression proof wage level being offered to Donald Macdonald to head his commission? Is it $800 a day? Second, would the Minister of Finance at least ask that commission to commence its activity at the earliest opportunity with a view to its advising the Minister on what course he should take to avert a still worse calamity in this country than is developing, and as to what he should do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, Royal Commissions do not come under my responsibility. The Hon. Member's question in that regard should be addressed to the Minister responsible for the Privy Council Office, namely, the Prime Minister.
As far as the Hon. Member's second point is concerned, the commission has been set up. Meetings have been held already. Last week Mr. Macdonald met with provincial Ministers and myself at the conclusion of the federal-provincial conference and there was a very helpful and fruitful exchange of views
with regard to the activities of the commission. I understand the commission is still in its organization stage. It is planning to proceed expeditiously with its plans of action, but again I think it would be raising false expectations and hopes to believe that this commission could come forth with recommendations for action in the next few months. That is the responsibility of the federal and provincial Governments of this country together with people in the private sector, both labour and management. That responsibility we are ready to assume. We have assumed it up to now, and we will continue to take the responsibility for it.

PURPOSE OF PRIME MINISTER'S FORTHCOMING VISIT TO FAR EAST
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. No doubt the Prime Minister is familiar with the OECD report to which I have referred, which lists his country, Canada, as number 24 out of 24 in terms of 1982 performance. Will the Prime Minister indicate why he feels that now is the time for him to take still another trip? In what way will that trip help the unemployed of this country?
Statistics Canada's figures issued this morning show that some of our industrial sectors are operating at only 51 per cent capacity and, on average, are operating at only 67 per cent. The OECD report has indicated that our downturn has been due to the postponement or cancellation in part of major energy projects in Canada. In that context, would the Prime Minister indicate how he might be able to do more to help the unemployed than by taking another trip?

subsubtopic: CLOSING OF RCA PLANT IN MIDLAND, ONT.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who, I believe, is engaged in conversation. If I could have him stand down, I have a question with respect to the electronics industry. The Minister will know that RCA in Midland, Ontario, the last electronic picture tube manufacturer in Canada, will shut down completely by the end of the year. That plant closing alone represents a loss of 1,200 jobs to the Canadian electronics industry. What efforts has the federal Government made in the past two or three years to support and strengthen the electronics industry in Canada?

Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Canada's import-export deficit in the electronics industry increased 15 per cent from 1980 to 1981. All the while the people in that industry are predicting that it could mean up to 100,000 to 150,000 jobs for Canadians in that industry by the end of the decade. What we want on this side is for those jobs to be in Canada and not offshore. What steps is the Canadian Government taking to ensure that those jobs are created in Canada and not offshore?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member knows, as do all Members of the House, that one-third of our total gross national product is dependent upon what we export abroad. Consequently we do not have the same flexibility that many other countries have with respect to having import regulations that keep products out of this country. He will also know from some of his own colleagues in the House, from the East and the West, that when we have taken steps, for example, in prohibiting cars from Japan coming to this country, they have requested that we eliminate those barriers and let those cars come in. subtopic: INCREASE IN PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
INCREASE IN PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who has been somewhat less than forthright with Parliament since he has not given us all the good news for Christmas. While Canadians from every region and virtually every walk of life are struggling during this depression period, the chartered banks of Canada have racked up fourth quarter profits that rank among the highest in their history. Return on fourth quarter average equity is in the 14.6 per cent range, with assets having grown similarly.
Will the Minister rise today and tell the House that he will meet with the chief executive officers of Canada's chartered banks and ask them to moderate their profiteering and join with the rest of Canada in trying to get the economy back on track?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCREASE IN PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a matter of fact I have already met with the banks. I discussed this subject in general terms a while ago. speechtext: That is the Bill you would not table.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Hon. Leader of the Opposition can show what he wants to do by what his Party is now prepared to do.
Last night we got this Bill through committee, and the Hon. House Leader of the Official Opposition suggested that the House today give report stage and third reading to this Bill, without debate. We hope that we may have unanimous consent from both Opposition Parties to do this.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I did not expect this kind of underhanded tactics from the Minister of Justice today. First they want us to pass second reading without even knowing what is in the Bill, without even having an opportunity to read it. Now they want us to pass it through report and third reading stages, without even having a word to say about it.
Had he been in consultation, which I am sure he was, with his colleague, the Government House Leader, he would have known the extent to which we are prepared to co-operate in getting this legislation passed. He would have known that we were prepared, and are prepared now. If he is listening he might consult with his colleague, the Government House Leader. We are prepared to deal, on this short day, with all remaining stages of that Bill, and see to it that it passes today.
I have had some consultations with gentlemen in the other place, and they assure me that it presents them with no problem if they get the Bill today.
In that spirit of co-operation, we make that offer to the Government.
The alternative would be to go on to Bill C-131 today, which is a lost day in any event because we know that that legislation is not going to pass today. If the Government is really sincere about wanting the human rights legislation, they will call it as the first order of business today. It will be dealt with today and dealt with, as I said last night, expeditiously.
There is another alternative. If they wish to call the human rights legislation first, I still assure the Government House Leader that we will deal with it expeditiously to the point where there will still be time remaining in the day to go back to Bill C-131, if that is the Government's desire.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
the disabled, we are prepared, as I have said on a number of occasions starting as early as last Friday, to see this legislation become law before we leave today.

All the mouthings that we heard last week from the Members of that Party, including the Leader of the Opposition, were just that. They were empty mouthings. They have no intention of putting this Bill through before Christmas.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

In all my time here I have never seen it occur before that a Minister of Justice asks us to give second reading to a Bill without even giving us an opportunity to see it. Now the same Minister is asking us to pass it entirely, without our saying even a word on it. That is an abdication of our responsibility, were we to agree to it.

Hear, hear!

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, December 21, consideration of Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2), as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, and the motion of Mr. Dantzer (p. 21795).

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 had an opportunity last evening to begin work on my remarks on Bill C-131, but before I start I would like to say a few words about what has transpired in the House in the last hour. 1 think all of us, including myself, would have to admit that the last hour was not spent in as desirable a fashion as we might have wished for this House of Commons. In many ways, we are looking at reform of the rules of the House, and 1 would submit, Mr. Speaker-I see you sitting on the edge of your chair. 1 do not know whether it is in anticipation of what I am going to say or whether you are going to rule me out of order in terms of context. Very briefly, we are looking at reform of the rules, and I would submit that one of the biggest reforms which all Members have to look at is a change of the attitude which we bring to this place. I would hope when we go home for Christmas and our constituents tell us about the many kinds of problems they are having in the real world, we will come back and carry on the affairs of the nation in a better fashion than we have in the past. I feel that is particularly incumbent upon the Government because it is the Government and it behooves it to set an example.
Which brings me to the concern which I have over Bill C-131, and particularly with the amendment to it. I see you are nodding your head, Mr. Speaker. I do not know if you are agreeing with me. I would suspect that you are, but probably you are hoping that I will return to the topic of the Bill.
Bill C-131, and particularly the amendment to it, which was moved by the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer), 15 a good amendment. 1 believe it is worthy of consideration and I would hope it is accepted by the Government, because essentially what it does, as I understand it, is it keeps the base under which the pensions will be calculated in the future moving through this inflationary period at the same rate it would have without Bill C-131. If in fact the Government has faith that the six and five program is going to work and that inflation will come down, then really it loses nothing in terms of Government expenditure if it accepts the Hon. Member's amendment. On that basis, 1 would submit it is a good amendment and it is one which would demonstrate that we in Canada have some responsibility and concern with the welfare of the senior citizens of this country who have been responsible for the kind of country we have been fortunate enough to be born in and live in. That is a very large debt which all of us owe to the people who have settled this country.
December 22, 1982

In many ways, they are the people who should be considered first and foremost when we are talking about Government expenditure.
I tried to point out last night that this is a very small amount of money relative to the total amount of money which this Government spends. I also pointed out that the highest figure 1 heard which the Government is proposing to save is something in the order of $80 million, although 1 do not think anyone knows what kind of saving there will be to the Government. It is roughly equivalent to the kind of money this Government, including Crown corporations, is spending on advertising, much of which is questionable advocacy advertising. It attempts to influence people's positions and attitudes. It is not informative advertising, specifically announcing Government programs so that people can take proper advantage of them. It is used by the Government to advocate its own position.
I submit that if the Government is serious about some of the expenditures it wants to cut back to get its deficit under control, there are other and more productive areas in which to cut back. This would create a better attitude amongst taxpayers because they would know the Government was spending its tax dollar more prudently.
Roughly $1 out of every $1,000 of Government expenditure is the largest potential saving under this Bill. The smallest potential saving is only $1 out of every $2,000 in Government expenditure. You have to remember that many of the people affected by this Bill are those who have homesteads on the land, they built log houses or sod houses, and they have had to chink the log houses against the winter weather. It is unfortunate the Government chooses to attack those people. I would much sooner see the Government concerned with productivity so that we can afford to have better pensions and social care assistance for our citizens. It seems to me that is the first responsibility of the Government.
There are many things the Government could be doing. One of the first things we should be looking at is the taxation system so that we encourage people to become more productive instead of penalizing them and thereby discouraging them from adding to our productivity. Instead of people being encouraged to look after themselves in their retirement years, they become more dependent on Government social assistance programs. Some of the tax regimes we have in place penalize people who try to look after themselves in their retirement years. The proposal in the November 12 budget whereby life insurance plans were going to be taxed on a three-year basis if they had some accrued value is one of those.
This Bill is really about inflation, Mr. Speaker. We would not have it if there was no inflation. When you look at the size of the deficits this country has been chalking up, you really wonder if anyone has been in charge of the economic ship of state in this country for the last ten or 15 years. We are at a point now where $1 out of every $4 collected in taxes goes to service past Government debt, and that money is then not available for social assistance programs which we all talk about in this House. It is money that is not available to provide
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Old Age Security benefits. Those are the kind of things we need to look at, and I submit, through better management of Government expenditure we would not have such a large Government debt and we would not be taking away from the private sector some of those savings I submit would be better used and better invested by individual Canadians to make this country more productive, enabling us to better distribute a larger pie among Canadians.
The Government is on the one hand saying that the six and five program is going to bring down inflation, but on the other hand it brings in legislation which forces people to accept some of the six and five restraint programs. That is almost an admission that the program will not succeed. If we were very confident that inflation was going to come down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the next two years, then we would not need legislation to force people to accept lower benefits from Government programs. If inflation is less than 6 per cent in the year Bill C-131 applies to, then the increase in the Old Age Security will be 6 per cent. So by the Government bringing in legislation such as this, in many ways it is admitting that the program is of questionable value. If inflation does come down to the level advocated in the six and five program, there really would not be a need for Bill C-131.
I received, as 1 think the rest of the Members of this House have, a very elaborately bound book with fancy leather like index tabs. It is about an inch and a half or two inches thick- I do not know what that is in metric, but it is a fairly thick binder. It outlines and extols the virtues of the six and five program. I wonder what the cost of that binder was and whether the money would be better spent by the Government in other areas or simply not spent at all. There are areas where this Government could, if it were serious, cut back on expenditures so we would not have to penalize the people affected by Bill C-131. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, the whole concept of the Government becoming more and more involved in regulating our daily lives, telling us what we can do, is counterproductive in many ways.
The province I come from, Saskatchewan, only became a Province in 1905, and there are people now living in that part of the country who were alive at that time. They are going to be affected by this Bill. I am sure of that because I know some of them. It seems to me that at that time there was a lot more room in this country for people to go out and work, sacrifice and achieve things on their own and keep some of the rewards for their own efforts and expertise. But what has happened in the interim is that governments have become so large that if you take the three levels of Government and look at the amount of taxes they take away from individual Canadians, it means that in many areas of the country you virtually work from the beginning of January until some time towards the middle of June for one level of Government or another. It seems to me that that is a kind of disincentive to the average taxpayer in this country to go out and work; he knows the Government is going to take such a large chunk of what he earns away from them and then redistribute it through various Government programs. That is a disincentive to individuals to

December 22, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
produce. When that happens we have to back up and take a look at the basic direction in which we are going.
Frankly, I do not understand some of the socialist thinking that goes on in this country. The average wage earner in this country, if he looks at where his money goes, will find his biggest cost is not fuel, food or rent, it is supporting one form of Government or another. That is the biggest deduction he has from his pay cheque each month. I fail to see why the socialists think the Government should take over more and there should be more taxation. It seems to me that the individual taxpayer in this country is perfectly capable of deciding where that money should be spent.
If you did leave one of those Canadians, those wage earners, those people who are productive, a little more money in his paycheque at the end of the week or at the end of the month, he would certainly spend that money. It would be recirculated through the economy, because we do have a circular economy. What is an expenditure for one of us is an income for the next person, if you did leave some additional income with Canadians, they would certainly spend it. They would not go home and burn the money in their basement after supper. They would recirculate that money. That is exactly what Governments have been trying to prevent, it seems to me, in the past number of years, in this country, when they take a larger and larger share of Canadians' earnings away from them, and redistribute it. This applies to all levels of Government, municipal, provincial and federal Government, all of them. If you look at some of the gross debts in this country and relate them back on a per capita basis, by and large, the federal Government does not set a good example. So when we say they are all involved, it does not mean that they are all equally complicit in this exercise. It simply means to me that the federal Government probably is setting a poor example for the various levels of Government.
I have heard many Government programs described, and one of the most humorous descriptions that I have heard, and an apt description in many ways, is that Government programs and Government grants are like taking a blood transfusion from one arm and moving it to the other arm, and spilling half of it on the way over. That is the problem we have with many Government programs, they get so large and so hung up with bureaucratic control and red tape that they lose sight of the purpose for which they were put in place in the initial stages.
Let me close by simply saying that I think the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Okanagan North is a very good amendment. It simply says to me that if the Government is serious and thinks it can bring inflation down to the 6 per cent range this coming year and the 5 per cent range the year following, the amendment will not cost the Government Treasury one cent. All it does is to keep the base against which future increases in the Old Age Security payments are calculated intact and keeps them moving through 1983 and 1984, as if this Bill had not been passed.
If in fact the Government believes that it can bring down the inflation rate in 1985 and 1986 to acceptable levels, and I assume by that that we are talking in the 5 per cent to 6 per cent range, the amendment will not cost the Treasury Board one single dollar.
I simply say in closing that if the Government believes its program is going to succeed, the Government would have no choice but to support the very well thought out and well put amendment by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North. I know I will have no trouble in supporting the amendment when it does come to a vote.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable patience the last two days to the discussion on Bill C-131, the Act that I feel is attacking senior citizens in this country, whether Members on the Government side believe it or not.
They seem to use as their argument that by reducing the anticipated increases in old age benefits to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the following year, they really are not cutting back. In fact, the Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) last night stated that we over here are using this as a political tool, I think was the phrase he used, to gain political points on the backs of senior citizens. That could not be further from the truth.
The amendment today introduced by the Member for Okanagan North, (Mr. Dantzer), indicates very clearly where we on this side of the House stand. The amendment only states in simple terms that the base for the senior citizen and the pensioner will not change.
I was particularly alerted by the remarks made by the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) last night. She said it was the duty of the Government to cut down inflation to six and five in all areas of the Government. That was used as justification for the attack on the senior citizens, people who are on fixed income and least capable of defending themselves.
She said there was an orchestrated campaign across the country to familiarize people with six and five. She said, and I am paraphrasing now, that a couple of months ago nobody knew what six and five was. I ask the Minister only one question. How much money was spent by the present Government to advertise six and five across the country, because the six and five program is a costly cop-out, and that is really all it is?
The six and five program is not lowering inflation or even beginning to, in this country. It is the policies of the Government that killed initiative and industry in this country, created unemployment and caused the situation where we have more unemployment in Canada today than we have had since 1932. That is what has caused the inflation rate to go down. Prior to the six and five program setting up wage limits on increases for public employees, private sector employees were receiving 3 per cent and 4 per cent increases, or no increases, or roll-backs in salaries, because of the economic times. The market looks
December 22, 1982

after itself in those areas, and all Hon. Members know that. They know that the six and five was planned in caucus, or by strategists, to focus the attention of Canadians on something else, to try to put across the nation that the Liberal Government was doing something, when in actual fact it is not doing anything. They are not living up to their responsibilities. They are not facing the hard issue, and that is the massive Government intervention in the economy, and the massive spending that costs nothing but dollars.
They have not faced up to the fact that the Crown corporations in this country, quoting the Auditor General's report, have created a hole in the pocket of the taxpayer and are costing the taxpayer of Canada millions and millions of dollars annually, with no control from the Government or this House of Commons.
We hear nothing of that and we will not hear anything of that. We will only hear chirping across the country, a massive advertising program across the country, at a cost to the taxpayers, six and five, six and five, six and five.
The Minister made a statement last night that the interest rate is lower than in past years. It is lower because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) who was then Minister of Energy, killed the economy in western Canada which was the oil or the lubricant to the economies of central Canada. His policies were responsible for driving people, investment and entrepreneurs out of the country and creating an atmosphere where there is absolutely no trust in the present Government. That is what has caused the massive unemployment across this country; and all Hon. Members in this House know that to be true.
The Minister again last night said that we have to make sure that we cut inflation to six and five in every area of Government that the Government can enforce. She said, seniors are fully protected. Seniors are not protected when you limit their base of income, and it falls below inflation, because the purchasing power of the dollar drops when inflation goes up. It is another insidious Government tactic.
Probably the most clear statement of the thinking of the Minister of National Health and Welfare last night was when she said "seniors will not shirk from their responsibilities." This is absolutely sad. It is indicative of the way the Government is going around, sending letters, publishing documents, talking to senior citizens and telling them to do their duty. These are the very people who built the country. They are the very people who, with their bare hands, cleared land and built the country. They are the people who, in any other society in the world, are revered because of the contribution they have made to their country. Certainly I agree with the Minister that seniors will rise and will not shirk from their duties because they know what duty is all about. But 1 think it is absolutely immoral for the Government to approach senior citizens along this line and say these kinds of things. These people have sacrificed all their lives raising families, putting them through school and university, often going without winter coats to keep the children in school. 1 know how my mother did without so
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
that I could have fresh fruit on the table. I know how my grandmother did without so that my mother could attend nursing school. 1 know that is part of the history of the country. It is immoral for the Government to attack senior citizens at this point.
But the Minister said that they had to have six and five in all areas which the Government controls. Let us look at some of the areas. Wage levels-Treasury Board announced on October 21 that 500 editorial employees of CBC would receive 11.5 per cent increases in their salaries ranging from $12,000 to $38,900. These people will receive 11.5 per cent increases in their salaries, yet the Government is limiting the indexing of the OAS for senior citizens who earn approximately $6,000. People on fixed rates of pay are generally low-income earners, while some 200,000 Government employees will receive 9 per cent or 10 per cent; if they are bumped up in category, the six per cent is added on and they receive 9 per cent or 10 per cent. These people can afford to bite the bullet a bit, but the Government attacks people on fixed incomes with the imposition of 6 per cent and 5 per cent.
Let us look at TransCanada Pipelines which just obtained a new levy for transporting natural gas. It was increased to 11.9 per cent on August 1. This will have a cumulative effect over the next two years with price increases of a further 93 cents per gigajoule in semi-annual steps of 23 cents and 24 cents per gigajoule. This will be a cumulative increase in the price of natural gas to consumers of 49.2 per cent. The same senior citizens who were encouraged to convert to natural gas are being told that their base pay will be limited, that it will not reflect inflation any longer so that they will have a minimum to live on or their purchasing power will not be eroded. They are being told that it will be nailed at six and five and that they will be charged an increase of 49.2 per cent in the cost of natural gas because the transportation costs of natural gas by TransCanada Pipelines have risen. We can depend on such things happening more and more.
Let us turn to rents under the direct control of the Government. The Minister said that the Government is responsible to Canadians. Also she said that they know and will do their duty, that they will limit every area to six and five, every area that they possibly can, every area under their control.
CMHC is the main renegade in this area. It is a federally-owned Crown corporation. Let us look at its increases-35 per cent in Coldbrook, Nova Scotia; 22 per cent in Churchill, Manitoba; 15 per cent in Winnipeg where CMHC administers the 180-unit Pine Hill Apartments; and 12.5 per cent for federal housing in the Northwest Territories. I put to Hon. Members that the people occupying those CMHC homes are the very ones who are being nailed here today; many of them are senior citizens. This is federally-controlled housing, it is immoral.
The very significant aspect about the figures I just gave is that most of the increases in rent apply to housing for public servants or those on fixed or limited incomes. Is that how the Government really attempts to nail six and five? It is nailing

December 22, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
the people who have the least voice in the House of Commons; that is whom it is hitting.
The federal Government talks about limiting to six and five, yet it turns around and increases the taxes for unemployment insurance levied against employers, including small employers, by 50 per cent next year. There are record bankruptcies and record failures in the small business sector, yet we have a Government saying that it will limit to six and five and increase the levy for unemployment insurance by 50 per cent. Who is kidding whom?
The Government of Canada is falsely going across the country and chirping six and five. It is a well-orchestrated campaign to sell Canadians on something which is just not so. Let us look at the passenger fares of VIA Rail. Were they increased by six and five? No way. There were 10 per cent increases in fares between Toronto and Montreal and between Toronto and Ottawa. The very people about whom we are talking today, the senior citizens, are the ones who predominantly use VIA Rail between those points. They are faced with a 10 per cent increase and a real purchasing power decrease.
I do not know what the decrease will be; none of us know because we do not know what will be the inflation rate in the next year. Mark my words, inflation will rise next year because it will be getting close to election time and the Minister of Finance will increase his deficit without decreasing his expenditures. He will try to heat up the economy and say to Canadians that they should look at the jobs which the Government created for the unemployed. He will not mention that this was a result of the Government's disastrous policies of before, but he will say, "Look at what we are doing; boy, are we leaders!" Then they will go into an election campaign. We can depend on it-inflation rates will go up next year. The real purchasing power of the senior citizen will go down.
I believe I have said all that I want to say except for one thing. I am getting sick and tired of listening to Members of the New Democratic Party standing up day after day on this Bill and accusing the Conservative Party of not caring. Because our Party voted on Bill C-124, which was a Bill to restrict Government spending to six and five per cent, the NDP has been twisting the meaning of that vote in an attempt to convince the Canadian public that our Party does not care, that we are only using this Bill for political purposes. Their Members have been questioning the motives of everyone who speaks on this Bill from our Party.
All I want to say to Members of the New Democratic Party is that they are not the only ones who have a licence for caring in this country. I care and all Hon. Members care when they go home and visit senior citizens' homes and the New Horizon drop-in centres. We talk to the seniors and we know instinctively the contribution they have made to our country. 1 am ashamed to go home and say to our seniors that we know they will come to grips with this matter and take part in the program, that they know their responsibility. 1 say we have a responsibility in this House to see that our senior citizens, the
people who contributed to our country, who built it and made it what it is today, do not want in their golden years. I plead with Hon. Members: "For God's sake, let this amendment go through".

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few remarks on Bill C-131. For us in this Party the issue is very simple. The Government is introducing limitations on the indexing of Old Age Security to 6 per cent in 1983 and to 5 per cent in 1984. The immorality of this becomes very clear when you compare this Bill, which takes money away from our senior citizens, with the appointment today of Michael Pitfield to the Senate.
The New Democratic Party is opposed to this Bill. We are opposed because we have a long history of struggle for decent pensions. What we want to see is some pension reform that will help our seniors have a better life, not something that will project them backwards.
For us the issue is simple, but for the Tories the issue is not so simple. If we go back to last summer when the Government introduced its six and five program, the Leader of the Tory Party said that this was a step in the right direction. The Tories are hesitating now when they see where the next step leads. The Tories are doing a hesitation waltz with the Government.
It was interesting to listen to the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) who was, ostensibly, opposing this Bill also and supporting the amendment. But he could not do so without introducing a few gratuitous comments about the whole failure of the idea of redistribution, nor without suggesting that somehow seniors should be able to look after themselves a little bit better on their own.
The reason for this Bill was given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). She said that the budget takes as a given fact that Canadians who are not in need are entirely prepared to share in serious sacrifices which are required to bring our country out of the economic crisis. In that short statement there are two serious misconceptions. The first is when she suggests that seniors who will be affected by this Bill are not in need. Second, she pretends that this mean, chiselling act directed at the elderly will somehow help to bring Canada out of its economic crisis.
In one respect the Minister's statement is right on. It finally recognizes that Canada is indeed in an economic crisis. 1 think it was President Nixon-it could have been Gerald Ford-who a few years ago visited a large American university where the agricultural faculty had managed to raise a 75-pound turkey. This poor, helpless creature had been forced-fed with hormones, steroids and other additives until it was so big that it could no longer walk. It could hardly stand. Nixon looked at the bird for a while and then reached deep into his bag of cliches and came up with this one: "This is the sort of thing that has made America great".
In a funny kind of a way, there is truth to that. This helpless 74-pound turkey symbolizes the Canadian economy as it has
December 22, 1982

developed over the last few years under the Liberal Government. The way the Canadian economy has developed has made America great. Over the last few decades, the Liberals have adopted an economic policy through which they felt they could manage to provide welfare measures and redistributive measures, such as the Family Allowance, Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, by having an economy which was based, first, on the export of our natural resources and, second, on branch plant manufacturing.
Today that 74-pound turkey can no longer support even its own weight. With two million people unemployed, goods and services are no longer being produced, tax revenues are down and the deficit climbs. What is the Government's response to that? The response is to cut back on the money that would have been paid in Family Allowances, in public servants' pensions and in Old Age Security.
These measures represent an insidious erosion and undermining of the right of seniors to live in dignity and to share in the wealth that our society has created and which they have helped to create. The New Democratic Party has a policy of full support for the principle of full indexation. Indexation is a very basic principle. It simply means that seniors with pensions should be able to buy the same basket of groceries in 1983 that they could buy with their pension in 1982. Bill C-131 will not make that possible because it says that regardless how high inflation goes-and no one expects it will stay as low as 6 per cent-pensions cannot increase by more than the 6 per cent factor.
It is important for us to realize that cutting back on pensions will not do anything for our economic crisis. There are no new jobs in this proposal. There is no increased production, nor is there any increased tax revenue. There is only a minuscule, miserly reduction in the $23.6 billion deficit. If the Government took the $105 million it claims this proposal will save over the next two years and applied the $105 million to this year's deficit, it would reduce the deficit from $23.6 billion to $23.5 billion. Our senior citizens are being punished. I suggest that rather than solving the economic crisis, Bill C-131 will make it worse.
In my riding, which comprises the southern part of Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, which is one of the more attractive places to live in Canada, there are some 11,000 people over the age of 65 who receive Old Age Security. I presume that roughly half of them do not get the Guaranteed Income Supplement. This means that between 5,000 and 6,000 senior citizens in my riding will receive less next year under Old Age Security than they would if the Government was not pushing this legislation through the House. At a time when our forest industry on Vancouver Island is reeling from massive unemployment, the income of senior citizens is the only factor that promotes any kind of economic stability in our area. The majority of these people have modest incomes.
As 1 said, Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, are good areas to retire and many pensioners were able to get modest homes. They do not have to live in extreme poverty in most
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
cases because of the past struggles of people like the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Seniors do live in poverty in the large cities but this is not true in most cases in our area. However, very few are in a situation where they do not need to count the nickels and dimes and dollars very carefully every day in order to have enough at the end of the month to meet their expenses. This Bill will make it that much more difficult for them to meet those expenses each month.
This is an insidious Bill because its effects will not be noticed immediately. Slowly but surely it will undermine the income of these people and of seniors who will follow to the point where they will have a lower place in the economic spectrum than they already occupy. We want to see their position improved, not degraded.
It is estimated that even with 10 per cent and 9 per cent inflation which has been estimated to occur next year and the year after, approximately $300 will be taken from seniors over the next two years. This is money which they should receive in order to keep up with inflation. The Government has said that inflation is coming down and that we will be living in the wonderful world of six and five. If it is true that inflation is really coming down to 6 per cent as the Government pretends, then Bill C-131 is unnecessary.
It is a fact that pensions have followed inflation. The whole idea of indexation is to allow pensions to follow inflation. It is completely wrong to suggest that pensions themselves have fueled inflation. On this basis, cutting pensions is in no way the answer to fighting inflation. Bill C-131 is penalizing the very people who need the money the most if inflation is not reduced to 6 percent. They are the very people who are having the most difficulty keeping up with inflation. This Bill is forcing the victims of inflation to pay for it. Therefore, this Bill is either unnecessary or unjust.
We want to stress that by capping indexation for the next two years, the Government is not only reducing pensions in 1983 and 1984, but also reducing the base on which future indexation will take place. For this reason we support the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer), which will include the amount to be lost from the pension base in 1983 and 1984 in the base for 1985 and following years. In other words, the purpose of this amendment is to ensure that even though the incomes of seniors will be reduced in 1983 and 1984, the base will continue to be built up by full indexation so that if and when indexation is restored in 1985 it will be operating on a full base.
Perhaps we should question whether there will be a reintroduction of full indexation. When one considers that this Bill is essentially doing nothing for the economy in terms of cutting back the deficit or making money available for other projects, perhaps the Government is simply introducing six and five now as the thin edge of the wedge and we will see a gradual and continuing cutback of the amount of money that is paid out through Old Age Security. On that basis, this Bill is mostly regressive.

December 22, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
The Government has pointed out that people who are in the lowest income brackets would have their Guaranteed Income Supplement increased by the amount that Bill C-131 takes away from their Old Age Security. While this is a positive measure, it involves two serious shortcomings. First, it penalizes most heavily those seniors who are just above the line in terms of having an income which disqualifies them from the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Bill C-131 cuts their pensions and they cannot make it up through the provisions to beef up the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
Second, this Bill, through its provisions to compensate for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, signifies a growing reliance on the means test. When old age pensions were first introduced in the late twenties, they involved a very stingy and chiselling type of means test. We eliminated that test and we do not want to see it reintroduced.
At present, more than 50 per cent of Old Age Security recipients also receive all or part of the Guaranteed Income Supplement which involves a form of means test. As a result of eroding the Old Age Security, Bill C-131 will force more people into the economic situation where they need the income supplement with the attendant means test. This means that the Government is moving away from the whole concept of universality. In future when the Minister of National Health and Welfare speaks about universality, when Canadians hear her they will hear her in much the same way they hear President Reagan speak about peace, Gerald Bouey speak about the problems of unemployment or the Tories speak about Party unity. In other words, they will hear these words as nothing more than lip service.
In conclusion, I suggest this Bill is not the answer. It penalizes our senior citizens and does nothing for the economy. At a time when our economy needs a transfusion of new blood, as it were, the Government comes in with medieval leeching practices, feeling that perhaps the answer to the sick economy is to draw more blood out of it. Over the next two years it will be taking $105 away from senior citizens.
The answer should be found, perhaps, in a new doctor, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) hesitated to suggest the other night. Yes, we do need a new doctor. We are tired of being leeched. We would like to see a doctor who could do something to build up the health of the economy instead of tear it down. We need a Government which will get our economy moving and provide opportunities for people to work again, thus providing revenue to the Government. When that happens, we will see our deficit come under some kind of control, and the Government will not have to penalize our senior citizens as a phony excuse for saying that it is doing something about the economy.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to make some comments with regard to Bill C-131. an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act.
Many of my colleagues have addressed the House on this matter and, I believe, have made very salient comments indeed on this Bill. I think it is now time that Hon. Members of the governing Party participate in a lesson in history. In the early 1920s, some 63 years ago, a generation of young Canadians, men and women, were celebrating victory in World War I, the first war to end all wars. Unfortunately, their efforts in the late twenties, in the business of rebuilding the economy, suffered a great blow in the depression which followed. Those who were fortunate enough to survive began rebuilding from the virtual ashes of our country.
Then in the late thirties and early forties, they again answered the call to arms and defended our freedoms and rights in the trenches of Europe and the rest of the world. All that kept some of our soldiers sane were their dreams. They dreamed of coming back to their loved ones and settling down in homes of their own. They were prepared to give their lives for their rights to liberty and justice. They were the people who guaranteed us the rights we have today.
When the Second World War ended, it was supposed to end all wars. Returning veterans and their colleagues who had supported them at home once again set about the task of rebuilding. Our Governments since then have realized the importance these people played in developing the institutions and, indeed, the bureaucracies of today.
The social security system was set up to protect our aging nation builders. These people are the ones whose incomes do not deserve to be protected against inflation, as the Government is now telling them through this Bill. Recently I had a

December 22, 1982

conversation with a retired Department of National Defence employee. Ele was indignant that he will be hit twice by this Government's last gasp efforts to play the role of the Grinch who stole Christmas. His comment was; "I worked 40 years to be robbed".
May I remind the House that most senior citizens today are quite a happy group of individuals. According to a recent survey, what they prize most is housing. Some say that this is because they spend more time indoors. I think it goes much deeper than that. The dream I mentioned of the soldier in the trenches was just to earn a living so as to own his own home for his family. This was the dream of all Canadians up until a few years ago when our population became so mobile. The current administration has stood idly by and allowed the cost of living to rise so rapidly that most younger Canadians have given up that dream. It existed, however, for all or more of our working lives.
Those who now own their own homes or are in comfortable accommodation are not expecting overnight solutions to our economic problems. They know from experience that there are no magical spells by which any Government can cure a depression. People realize, too, that there are more senior citizens per capita in Canada today than ever before. The baby boom was turned into the senior boom. They know there is strength in numbers.
The Government must admit that it is not keeping inflation down to the proposed 6 per cent and 5 per cent, partially due to the cost of imported foods which comprise a great portion of the goods in our shopping carts. This is uncontrollable and also partially due to the fact that senior citizens themselves have allowed for some salary increases above 6 per cent or 5 per cent. Senior citizens are quite willing to pay their share to keep the country, which they built, growing. They have done so in their working years and do not expect any less now. Now, however, they are forced to accept cost of living adjustments below that allowed, in some cases, to federal Government employees.
I would like to refer back to the example of the shopping cart in the grocery store to which we must all go once a week or more. Our lifestyle has changed because we are now importing far more food than we did years ago. It has become very essential in the diet of senior citizens. They are being penalized as a result of the worth of the Canadian dollar in comparison to the American dollar, the cost of importation, the cost of handling, transportation and oil prices.
We must also remember what the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) said yesterday with respect to a number of senior citizens. He said that the fact is that in the last ten years the number of Canadians under the age of 20 years has dropped by over 700,000 and the number of Canadians over the age of 60 years has grown by 800,000. We are seeing a basic change in the age of the population in Canada. This is an important factor in how we consider the programs and social needs of Canada in the coming years.
One of the major social problems we face is the persistence of poverty. At this point in time, at least, 15.5 per cent of our population can be described, on the basis of certain income
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
levels, as being below the poverty line. Must senior citizens be forced to accept such low cost of living adjustments? This they might well pass off as being the antics of a Government which will go eventually. Many others have come and gone in their lifetime. They are constantly reminded, however, of the inequities demonstrated by the Government. The Government has estimated that it will save approximately $100 million by deindexing Old Age Security payments, yet its deficit is 230 times greater. Obviously, such saving will not even be seen, it will be spent so fast.
My constituents from Lindsay, Keswick, Haliburton and many other parts of my vast riding have written to me many times concerning metric conversion. I defy the Minister responsible to prove to me that the cancellation of the metric conversion program would not result in a much greater saving to the public purse than will be accomplished by Bill C-131, and with much less harmful effects. It is my opinion that being forced to metric conversion is one of the easiest ways to confuse people in the marketplace.
Metric conversion, as I said earlier, is very, very confusing, not just in the gasoline stations but in the grocery business itself. By forcing people to go metric on January 1, the cost of the scales and the other measures which will follow will certainly add to the cost of the shopping basket. Regardless of what some people would like us to believe, this is a very costly experience for Canada. I have been told that it has cost us over $1 billion thus far in the implementation of the metric system, and what are we going to gain? Our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his campaign promises in the late election, promised that he would wrestle inflation to the ground. Congratulations, Mr. Prime Minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to have this opportunity on the last day of the session of the House before the Christmas recess to take part in this debate on Bill C-131. I would like to make some comments by way of rebuttal of some remarks which have already been made, and indicate where I feel some of the error lies with this piece of legislation. I make that comment having regard to the fact that I was one of the first Members on this side of the House who

December 22, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
supported what has been referred to as the "six and five solution". 1 do not know that one should automatically assume that, when a piece of legislation is presented to the House which has merit and happens to have contained therein a particular formula, a simple snapping of the fingers to resurrect that formula when applied to any other piece of legislation should result automatically in someone concluding that Hon. Members will support the legislation in a sort of "knee-jerk" reaction to the Bill which is introduced.
Very clearly, Bill C-124, which began the process, was a Bill designed to meet a certain set of circumstances which affected, among other people, Members of this House of Commons. Members of the House have been entitled to an indexed form of remuneration increase on an annual basis, and I found it extremely difficult to sit here and vote in favour of a constant increase in my salary as a Member of Parliament while my constituents suffered from lack of employment.
1 also found it quite easy to justify the imposition of a form of restrained growth in salaries for members of another privileged class, the Public Service, and there is no doubt but that they are. They have an opportunity to continue to serve the public without the same general fears of possible loss of employment which are imposed upon members of the private sector. We have seen hundreds of thousands, possibly two million of those persons who no longer have employment at all, and yet within the Public Service we know that security of employment must be given some monetary value. Quite frankly, 1 felt no hesitation at all in supporting Bill C-124.
1 do, however, have substantial reason for opposing Bill C-131, despite the fact that it also has a six and five formula appended to it. The reason is very simple. We are dealing in this piece of legislation with an element of society which has withdrawn from the work force. We are dealing with a group of Canadians who no longer are in a position to make up in the long run what might be lost today. We are dealing with people who have paid their dues to society, who have contributed to the very essence of our nation, who have contributed to the fact that we are here today in this place, free and secure. These are the people to whom we, as a society, have an obligation, and that obligation transcends any consideration of monetary restraint. They are indeed, in my mind, the most deserving class in society to whom we, as Members of Parliament, should pay tribute for their contribution to our society, and regard in a special fashion when it comes to dealing with rights to which they have become entitled.
In terms of the actual consequences of this legislation, we were advised just this week that the inflation rate has declined and that decline now is measured at 9.8 per cent on an annual basis. The income increase under this Bill is fixed at 6 per cent. So we are now looking at a 3.8 per cent decline in an increase.
I use those words because that in fact is what it is in terms of today's dollars. But in terms of constant dollar valuation, there is clearly a reduction in the purchasing power of those pension payments which are made available to our senior citizens as a consequence of this legislation. For that reason, and for the reasons I have earlier described in terms of our obligation to
this segment of society, I am opposed to the Bill and will vote against it.
I would like to mention some of the concerns which I have had with respect to the Government's defence of this legislation. I recognize that it is part of a program designed to dilute the expectation for constant inflationary increases in society. The Government also regards it in some way as an indication of its grappling with the control of the public purse, hopefully achieving a reduction in federal expenditures, and they have done so at the cost of a particular segment of society, as 1 have indicated. If you analyze the growth of the inflationary pressures, you find that the chief culprit is not simply the Government. It is Government in the sense that one of the large component factors in the increase in the consumer price index is the cost of energy. Cost of energy is reported to have accounted for an 18.2 per cent increase over the year. With that kind of an increase, controlled by Government, one can well understand how there is a reduction, as reported in the press recently, of the inflationary pressures. That reduction is retarded because Government is still intruding in a fashion which in itself creates the very inflationary pressures they have come to blame on society at large.
We are also aware of the recent increases in excise taxes imposed on those evil products of tobacco and alcohol, taxes which were not restricted to six and five but which are running at almost 14 per cent. Now, I know that not everyone needs a smoke or a drink, but I find it a little hypocritical for the Government to come before the public and say: "We expect you to do your part, while we do not do ours". An example is the Government saying that it has begun to restrain the demand upon the public purse, yet we see the kind of treatment accorded another group of special people, the senior bureaucrats, and in particular a certain Senator Michael Pitfield who a short time ago was awarded a special pension arrangement which will see the extraction from that same public purse of some $100,000 over a period of years to be added to Mr. Pitfield's pension plan.

However, having regard to the way in which he served so faithfully the current Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), he has been rewarded in a fashion which 1 am sure most Canadianss would like to tap into but which is not available to them, certainly not to the people affected by Bill C-133. For them they are prepared to make some different arrangements. Those are the kinds of things which surely make the public sit up and take notice and regard Government actions with a great deal of disbelief.
December 22, 1982

Now, I listened with some interest to the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) when he commented disparagingly upon the part our Party has played with respect to this legislation. 1 say that our Party has been very straightforwd in its condemnation of what must be regarded as special treatment for special people by the Government. That special treatment should be accorded to those most deserving in society, that group 1 have just identified.
I find it rather interesting that the NDP has consistently adopted a policy of spending money, indexing everything, without regard to the source of funds. Their lack of recognition of the need to take that into account is clearly best demonstrated by the public recognition of that failure and their regard among the general public as most recently displayed in the public opinion polls. If I could pass on advice to Members of that Party who wish to in any way enhance the public's view of their performance, let me suggest they be more reasonable and sensible and account for the fact that they are constantly deciding to spend and index without paying any attention to the consequences of their actions. 1 believe that once you spend a dollar, the dollar cannot be spent again unless you borrow it and pay interest on it. That is a policy which has, unfortunately, been adopted by the Government.
Now, last month there were two Bills before this House, Bill C-129 and Bill C-130, dealing with rather substantial amounts of money. The first Bill dealt with the advancing of no less than $1.7 billion to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and I heard not one whisper from Members to my left as to how that money might well have been redirected to helping the very people whom they are now complaining are not receiving these funds. Members of this Party spoke about that, about how this money was leaving Canada for international financial institutions without any hope of control by this Parliament or the Government over how the money was to be spent. How that money was to be spent was beyond our control. I could not conceive for one moment why Members of the NDP were not jumping up and down in their place demanding that that subtantial sum be directed to the payment of the indexing of pensions plans for senior citizens.
Immediately following that Bill's passage, we were confronted with Bill C-130 which provided for the incurring of an obligation in the aggregate amount of $117 million. In this case the funds were to be paid at the discretion of the Government to a number of international banks. Once again, there was not one whimper of objection from the NDP. The policy that that Party has regretfully followed is best illustrated by the fact that when money is being spent, regardless of for what, they favour it. However, when there is a curtailment in expenditures with a view to controlling the deficit and reducing the cost of financing the national debt, the Members of that Party consistently clamour against the legislation. It makes it extremely difficult for a prudent public to be able to distinguish between what actions they adopt as correct and what actions they adopt as incorrect.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I favour the position of opposing legislation which has the effect, unreasonably, of extracting funds from the Consolidated Revenue Fund which will not benefit Canadians. 1 favour legislation where we have a good moral or business reason for favouring the expenditure. In this case, Mr. Speaker, I certainly favour the position of opposing this specific piece of legislation encompassed within the confines of Bill C-131, for the reasons I have given.
In opposing this legislation I am perfectly consistent with the views I have expressed about helping Canadians first. Among those Canadians we should help are those who have served their country long, who are no longer in a position to contribute in the same fashion as others to their welfare and have become entitled to special protection from this place and other Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been sitting here for several weeks listening to this debate and it behooves me to try to respond a little to some of the things that have been said. When we keep hearing people from both sides talking about how much of a Grinch we are, how we are so tight and cruel and so on, I have to respond because I think the facts are just not in that order. That is not the situation. This Government, one that 1 have been involved with for ten years, has been very, very supportive of Canadians in general, and particularly those Canadians who need more support than other Canadians. To say this is untrue is, to my mind, totally false and quite hypocritical.
I particularly find hypocrisy in the Tory Party very difficult to accept. I have heard Members from the other side rant and rave about Government spending and talk about their great model. I remember one of the Members from British Columbia and also the Opposition critic for finance preach that Reaganomics is the answer. They said that this was the approach that we should all take, that we should get Governments off our backs, and they talked about the great economic views of the President of the Unites States, views that we have come to know as Reaganomics.
I would just like to refer to a couple of articles dealing with Reaganomics, because this is the argument that has been made about this Government and its spending. It is an argument that, if the Tory Party believes in it, means they are really hypocritical in dealing with this Bill.
The first piece was from Houston dated June 15 and appeared in the New York Times. It says:
President Reagan returned to the Oval Office today for the first time since the start of his European trip two weeks ago but then flew here this afternoon for a rousing defence of his economic policies and some partisan blasts at his critics.
The occasion for Mr. Reagan's rally was a $1,000-a-plate dinner for 3,500 cheering, applauding Texans.
The next article is dated a few weeks later, July 19, from Newsweek, as follows:
Last April the Texas Department of Human Resources issued a pamphlet entitled "Dead Broke in Texas?" warning newcomers not to expect much in the way of public assistance. It points out that the average welfare and food-stamp

December 22, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
recipient in the state gets only $34 a month under each program and declares that qualification requirements are much "stiffer" than in other states.
That, I think, tells us a little about the Tories' way of speaking when they espouse Reaganomics. A one thousand dollar-a-plate dinner and 3,500 people show up-and the average welfare recipient in that city was receiving $68 a month!
It is in that context that I have to stand up and defend what we are doing. There are two basic pieces to this legislation, Bill C-131, Bill C-132 and Bill C-133, that have to be understood. The first piece has to be that in June of this year we put into play a program called six and five. It would not be of any value to have a program if we were going to say that we were going to have six and five for this but we were not going to have six and five for that; that we are going to make all kinds of exceptions, but somewhere along the line the program is called six and five. We hope to have a 6 per cent inflation rate and we are going to adjust Government spending to a 6 per cent inflation rate in the coming year and 5 per cent the following year.
To me, if we decided that we would exempt this group and that group, we would do two things. One is that we would deny the six and five; and, number two, if we were to say we will include this group but leave out that little group, then we would get away from a notion that I think is very important- universality. I will come to that later. 1 want to defend universality which is part of this kind of thinking here.
The second reason I think it is important that we have a total type of program and why this is not going to create a lot of hardship is simply that the inflation rate, in my opinion, is going down much faster than people believe. I do not for a minute say that six and five was the only or even the principal cause of this. I do say that the inflation rate in this country is coming down at a faster pace than people believe.
We unfortunately have a method of arriving at an inflation rate which I think is totally inadequate. It basically deals with the inflation rate in the past rather than the future. The Americans have a different system in that they tend to project more into the future and take a single month and annualize it more than we do. When we say the inflation rate this month is 9.8 per cent, we are talking about the month of December through November in 1981/1982; so in that inflation factor we are carrying several months, four, five or six months when the rate was in excess of 11 per cent, and in some of those months in excess of 12 per cent. The actual inflation rate since the announcement on June 28 of the six and five program is about 7.5 per cent, not 9.8 per cent as was announced last week.
One might say that if you annualize those 12 months you get 9.8 per cent; but the fact is that anyone who has looked at this thing at all realizes that there is a distinct decline in inflation rates, not just here but all around the world. Basically, we can expect this decline to get smaller.
One of the factors that would lead me to believe that there would be a further decline is that in that 7.6 per cent is included one of our two annual increases in energy rates. That is now
completely built into these figures. We have had, as I say, roughly a 7.5 per cent inflation rate since the last budget.
To look at next year, there are certain other factors that would probably cause the inflation rate to drop below 6 per cent, the most significant being the energy factor itself. We are coming very close to a situation where we are at 75 per cent of world price. We have some additional rounds built in, but these rounds will disappear if the world price comes down. The world price is conceded to be $40, but the spot price is considerably below that. One could expect the world price of oil to decline considerably and that we may not have any significant increases in our price. As a matter of fact, in early January one could expect a 1.5 cent per litre decline in oil prices, which was just announced by the Government. That decline may actually represent the major shift in the whole year.
We can see the evidence in terms of wages and other things. For example, when 1 go into a grocery store to buy meat today, 1 am paying less than I was paying some months ago. This varies from time to time, but certainly there is evidence that the inflation rate is coming down. Therefore, the factor about which we talk when we say that people will lose a great deal will not exist because the rate will come down.
1 have some sympathy with the last Hon. Member who said that, if the rate was to be 6 per cent or less, why do we need the Bill? We brought it in for one particular reason-to create the psychological climate which would cause this to happen. Once one moves in that direction, one follows through.
I am not convinced that the months of discussion on these three Bills was all that necessary, because in general people on fixed incomes who will receive the 6 per cent will be as well off as they were when they received 11 per cent. 1 say this because the inflation rate is coming down. If 1 were a betting man, I would bet very strongly that the inflation rate next year-and certainly going into the new year-will be down below 6 per cent. That idea can be justified economically on many grounds. One should look in that direction and see, therefore, that the Bill will not do damage to individuals.
There is another factor which I think we should be debating. 1 have been bothered that a great deal of the debate around here has been centered on a very small fraction of the inflation rate; probably one-half of 1 per cent or even no percentage point. The debate has been on that rather than the whole notion of universality. When 1 talked about the Reagan administration and the Tory defence of Reaganomics over the last year or two, 1 used this example to show that we as a Government have not contemplated and were not contemplating any move which would take away the factor of universality.
